body.text: The tenure of Balendra Shah as Nepal’s prime minister started with the twin arrests of former Prime Minister KP Sharma Oli and his Home Minister Ramesh Lekhak. The two were accused of trying to suppress the September 2025 Gen Z uprising, during which at least 76 people died. Then Shah moved to clear riverside squatters in Kathmandu. Both these decisions were deemed questionable and overturned in court.
But such legal hurdles have not stopped Shah, the 36-year-old prime minister who was the de facto leader of the uprising, from continuing to test the limits of executive power.

His government has since decided to send scores of senior bureaucrats into early retirement, without much consultation. The government bypassed the long-accepted seniority rule in the appointment of the Supreme Court chief justice. It has even detained journalists and sent police into newsrooms – things were this bad for the Nepali press only during the autocratic royal regime back in the early 2000s.

Most recently, the government fired Dan Bahadur Karki, the police chief who was reluctant to take direct orders from the Prime Minister’s Office (PMO). In all these cases, Shah, who came to power on the back of an anti-corruption and good-governance platform, seemed intent on giving short shrift to due process as he went about “cleaning up” the government.

Such routine overstepping of executive authority has eroded public confidence in the government that came to office on the back of an overwhelming mandate in the March 2026 elections. It has also progressively alienated Rabi Lamichhane, the chair of the ruling Rastriya Swatantra Party (RSP).

Shah, naturally reclusive, leads the government through a coterie of advisors. As the RSP chief Lamichhane sees it, Shah has bypassed the party and even his ministers on important decisions. In the parliamentary system Nepal has adopted, it is difficult for the prime minister to govern effectively without a high level of support from their mother party.

As far as Shah is concerned, there is nothing new about his modus operandi. Previously, as the mayor of Kathmandu, he refused to be bound by the law, whether it came to sending bulldozers to tear down squatter settlements or dumping garbage in front of the central secretariat to show his displeasure with the federal government. He never gave interviews and what little people heard of him was through short social media posts.

Through his laconic style, he had cultivated an air of mystery. People loved the young, rapping engineer, who seemed incorruptible and capable of getting things done in a country notorious for slow government work. Shah now seems to be trying to apply the same formula as the prime minister.

But the expectations and responsibilities of a mayor and those of a prime minister are vastly different. The mayor enjoys a high level of autonomy and is expected to independently develop their local jurisdiction. The prime minister, on the other hand, is answerable to the parliament that elects him. The PMO, in fact, cannot function without a high level of cooperation and coordination with a wide set of actors. It also naturally attracts a lot more scrutiny and is held to higher standards of accountability than that of the mayor’s.

Yet the prime minister and his supporters seem to believe that it is not just Shah’s promises that were endorsed in the March polls. It was also his style of governing as the mayor of the national capital. Voters saw established procedures and institutions as shields for corruption, delay and inaction.

There is some truth to that. But the downsides of rushed decisions are also becoming clear: risk of judicial reversal, officials afraid of making decisions for which they might later be held accountable, institutional decay, and lack of cooperation all around.

It would also be a mistake to assume that people will continue to unquestioningly back Shah. The same social media and YouTube voices that once lauded him are now calling for accountability, for instance, over a controversial audio that has surfaced linking the prime minister to an infamous “fixer.” The government’s crackdown on free speech has been widely condemned, as has the tendency of the prime minister’s advisers to dress down senior civil servants. Likewise, the business community is disillusioned. There is disquiet even in the RSP at the government’s functioning.

It would be a tragedy if the RSP government fails because of these missteps and miscalculations. The party got an overwhelming mandate because of the mistrust of the old political forces—a mistrust that culminated, tragically, in the Gen Z uprising. The corrupt old guard was thrown out, and in its place came a cohort of young and ambitious parliamentarians and ministers.

If he is not careful, Shah risks wasting this rare mandate. He and his advisers must understand that urgency does not mean dispensing with consultation or due process. Being mindful of these constraints will strengthen his government’s democratic credentials and increase his ability to deliver.

The failure to do so, on the other hand, could prove fatal to Shah’s premiership. More importantly, with the new forces seemingly no different from the old ones they threw out, the Nepali people’s faith in the democratic process will be badly dented.
